idiom_name: marker types (empty structs / PhantomData) selected by trait resolution
implementation_notes: The idiomatic Rust form: the choice lives in the type system as a marker type, the implementation is selected by trait resolution and baked in by monomorphization, so no vtable and no tag value exist at run time. PhantomData lets a tag parameter ride along without occupying storage, which is how the choice is threaded through structs that otherwise do not use it. Choose it whenever the decision is expressible as a trait bound - that is almost always, and it is the only form that works inside generic functions.
pitfalls: Monomorphization duplicates the body per instantiation: a wide type matrix costs binary size and compile time, and unlike C# the compiler gives no shared fallback for reference types.
Adding a new impl can change which method an existing call resolves to when trait and inherent methods share a name - inherent methods win, and re-exported blanket impls can shadow user impls.
Marker types cannot carry data; a tag that needs a value has to become a real field, which changes the layout the pattern existed to avoid.
sources: The Rust Programming Language, Generic Data Types (monomorphization and zero-cost static dispatch), https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch10-01-syntax.html

rs4ts, Specialization (stable Rust: a trait with a default method overridden per type replaces overlapping impls; dispatch resolved at compile time via monomorphization), https://rs4ts.dev/25-advanced-topics/07-specialization/

variants.name: Autoref/autoderef specialization (method-resolution priority ladder)
variants.idiom_name: traits implemented on &T / &&T so that the fewest-autoref candidate wins, returning tag types
variants.implementation_notes: Where the ladder needs 'if the type implements X use that path, otherwise fall back', stable Rust can borrow method-resolution priority: a method reachable with fewer autorefs wins, so an impl on &T is only reached when the impl on T does not apply, and autoderef chains generalize it to arbitrarily many ordered levels. Because the ladder must see the concrete receiver, it only works from macros (resolution inside a generic function uses the declared bounds), and the usual shape returns a tag type so that the real work can dispatch a second time on it.
pitfalls: The priority order is first-come-first-served, not specificity: putting the general case first means the specific case is never selected, the opposite of how specialization would behave.
It is macro-only: from inside a generic function the compiler resolves against the bounds, so the technique appears to work in tests and silently takes the general path in a generic wrapper.

Inherent methods outrank trait methods and std blanket impls interfere with the reference impls; both hazards make the ladder fragile under refactoring and require a wrapper type and heavy commenting.
sources: David Tolnay, Autoref-based stable specialization (the original technique, method-resolution priority, macro-only limitation), https://github.com/dtolnay/case-studies/blob/master/autoref-specialization/README.md
pick_by_autoderef (docs.rs): 'Pick by Autoderef ... is strictly first come first served', exact receiver type required, https://docs.rs/pick-by-autoderef/latest/pick_by_autoderef/index.html
Faking Specialization on Stable Rust (tag types propagate the decision; macro use cases), https://blog.asteromorph.com/autoref/
